opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to separating what's essential from what's appealing.

The humanoid form is attractive for a clear reason. Our world was built around human bodies: door handles, stairs, kitchen counters, tools. So the argument goes that a robot shaped like us can slot into all of it without changing anything. That logic is real. But I think it's a long-term argument being applied to a short-term problem.

Right now, the bottleneck in robotics isn't the body. It's the brain: perception, manipulation, generalization, robustness when something unexpected happens. Most of the useful work we want robots to do is really about the hands and what's directly in front of them, like picking, placing, folding, assembling, wiping. You don't need two legs to do that. A wheeled base with one or two good arms covers a huge portion of real tasks. It's cheaper, more stable, safer around people, easier to maintain, and much easier to collect data with.

Legs are a good example. Bipedal locomotion is impressive engineering, but it adds a lot of cost and failure modes. You spend energy just staying upright, and a fall can damage the robot or hurt someone. For most indoor environments, wheels work fine. When you add legs, you're paying a big tax for a capability you often don't need yet.

There's also a data argument. If we believe progress will come from learning, from large amounts of real-world interaction, then we want platforms that can be deployed widely and cheaply so they generate experience. A simpler form factor gets you more robots, in more places, sooner, and that feedback loop matters more than resemblance to a human.

So I wouldn't say humanoids are wrong. They may well be where things converge eventually, once the intelligence is good enough that the body becomes the limiting factor. But at this stage I think the field should be form-agnostic and task-driven. Ask what the job actually requires, build the simplest body that does it well, and put most of the effort into the intelligence. The shape can come later.

r001.rationale: It says a wheeled base with one or two arms can handle many useful real-world tasks, such as picking, placing, folding, assembling, and wiping.

r002.rationale: It suggests humanoids may become suitable later, but does not say developers could adopt solutions after others solve humanoid-robot problems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd push back a little on the framing first, because the question I get asked is usually "why not humanoid," and I think the honest answer is that the humanoid form is a bet about the future, not a requirement of the present.

The argument for humanoids goes like this: the world was built for humans, so a robot shaped like a human can use every door, every staircase, every tool, every kitchen without us redesigning anything. That's a real argument, and over a long enough horizon I think it's probably right. But "the world was built for humans" is doing a lot of work in that sentence. What it really means is the world was built for human hands, human balance, human perception, and human judgment, all working together. A humanoid robot today has the silhouette of a human and almost none of those capabilities at human level. So you pay the full cost of the form, two legs that have to balance, a lot of joints, a high center of mass, expensive actuators, hard safety problems, and you get a fraction of the benefit.

Meanwhile, if you look at where robots are actually creating value right now, almost none of it requires a body like ours. Warehouse robots are flat boxes on wheels. Surgical robots are arms bolted to a table. Agricultural robots are tractors with vision. A robotic arm on a wheeled base with a decent gripper can already do a surprising amount of what people imagine a humanoid doing in a factory, and it does it cheaper, more reliably, and without the risk of falling over on someone.

The bottleneck at this stage isn't the body, it's the brain. Dexterous manipulation, understanding a messy environment, recovering from mistakes, those are the hard problems, and they're hard regardless of whether the robot has legs. So my view is: spend your effort where the bottleneck is. Pick the simplest body that gets the task done, collect data, make the intelligence better. Once the intelligence genuinely can exploit a human-like body, the humanoid form becomes worth its cost. Until then, it's mostly a very expensive way to look impressive on stage.

I'd add one more thing. Form should follow task, and a lot of tasks have a better form than human. A human is a generalist compromise. If your job is moving pallets, wheels beat legs. If your job is picking strawberries, a small, light arm beats a 60-kilogram torso. The humanoid wins only when the task set is broad enough that generality beats specialization, and that's a late-stage condition, not an early one.

r001.rationale: The response gives concrete useful examples that do not require humanoid forms, including warehouse robots, surgical robots, agricultural robots, and wheeled robotic arms.

r002.rationale: The response says humanoid robots may become worthwhile once intelligence improves, but does not suggest developers could adopt solutions to humanoid-robot problems after others solve them.

astra-6.text:
I think we should start with the task we want a robot to perform. Does it need to move boxes, inspect equipment, or clean a floor? Those tasks require different capabilities, and a human-shaped body isn’t necessarily the most efficient way to provide them.

For example, if the robot operates on a flat floor, wheels may be enough. Adding legs introduces challenges in balance, control, energy consumption, and reliability. You need a clear benefit to justify that complexity. The same applies to hands: some tasks need dexterity, but others can be done with a simple gripper.

The argument for humanoids is that our environments were built for people. That’s a reasonable argument, especially if you want one robot to perform many different tasks. But at the current stage, I would focus on getting a robot to do something useful reliably and at an acceptable cost. If that requires a humanoid form, use it. If it doesn’t, there’s no reason to make human appearance a requirement.

r001.rationale: It says wheels or a simple gripper may be sufficient for practical tasks such as moving boxes, inspecting equipment, or cleaning, without requiring a human-shaped body.

r002.rationale: It does not suggest waiting for others to solve humanoid-robot problems before adopting their solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should start with the task we want a robot to perform, rather than assume it needs to look like a person. A humanoid form makes sense in some situations, especially when the robot has to use spaces and tools designed for humans. But it also introduces a lot of complexity: balancing, coordinating many joints, and managing power consumption.

If the job is moving goods around a warehouse, wheels and a suitable lifting mechanism may do that more reliably and at a lower cost. You don’t necessarily need two legs and two arms.

At this stage, I think the priority is getting robots to do useful work consistently. Let the task determine the form. As the technology improves, a humanoid design may become the right choice for more applications, but it doesn’t have to be the starting point.

r001.rationale: It says robots can do useful work in nonhumanoid forms, giving wheeled warehouse robots as an example.

r002.rationale: It says humanoid designs may suit more applications as technology improves, but does not suggest developers can adopt solutions after others solve humanoid-robot problems.
